section.title: The Day of Atonement
section.sectionRationale: This is the central, climactic ritual of Leviticus, given after the death of Nadab and Abihu and the purity laws of chapters 11 through 15, the once a year answer to accumulated sin and uncleanness, standing just before the Holiness Code begins in chapter 17.
section.thesis: On the Day of Atonement, once each year, the high priest enters the Most Holy Place with blood to atone for himself, the sanctuary, and all the people, while a second goat visibly bears their sins away into the wilderness, foreshadowing Christ's once for all atonement and the complete removal of sin.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the warning after Nadab and Abihu and Aaron's careful entry; the blood of the bull and the goat sprinkled in the Most Holy Place; the scapegoat sent away bearing Israel's sins; and the permanent statute establishing an annual day of atonement.

units.label: Not freely, but carefully
units.note: after the death of two sons

media.alt: A veiled entrance before the ark
media.caption: Aaron may not enter the Most Holy Place freely, only as commanded, and once a year.

verses.text: Now the LORD spoke to Moses after the death of two of Aaron’s sons when they approached the presence of the LORD.

And the LORD said to Moses: “Tell your brother Aaron not to enter freely into the {{qodesh|Most Holy Place}} behind the veil in front of the {{kapporet|mercy seat}} on the ark, or else he will die, because I appear in the cloud above the mercy seat.
This is how Aaron is to enter the Holy Place: with a young bull for a sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering.

He is to wear the sacred linen tunic, with linen undergarments. He must tie a linen sash around him and put on the linen turban. These are holy garments, and he must bathe himself with water before he wears them.
And he shall take from the congregation of Israel two male goats for a sin offering and one ram for a burnt offering.

units.label: Two goats, one lot
units.note: for the LORD, and for the scapegoat

verses.text: Aaron is to present the bull for his sin offering and make {{kipper|atonement}} for himself and his household.
Then he shall take the two goats and present them before the LORD at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.
After Aaron casts lots for the two goats, one for the LORD and the other for the {{azazel|scapegoat}},
he shall present the goat chosen by lot for the LORD and sacrifice it as a sin offering.
But the goat chosen by lot as the scapegoat shall be presented alive before the LORD to make atonement by sending it into the wilderness as the scapegoat.

units.label: Blood behind the veil
units.note: for himself, and for the people

verses.text: When Aaron presents the bull for his sin offering and makes atonement for himself and his household, he is to slaughter the bull for his own sin offering.
Then he must take a censer full of burning coals from the altar before the LORD, and two handfuls of finely ground fragrant incense, and take them inside the veil.
He is to put the incense on the fire before the LORD, and the cloud of incense will cover the mercy seat above the Testimony, so that he will not die.
And he is to take some of the bull’s blood and sprinkle it with his finger on the east side of the mercy seat; then he shall sprinkle some of it with his finger seven times before the mercy seat.

Aaron shall then slaughter the goat for the sin offering for the people and bring its blood behind the veil, and with its blood he must do as he did with the bull’s blood: He is to sprinkle it against the mercy seat and in front of it.

So he shall make atonement for the Most Holy Place because of the impurities and rebellious acts of the Israelites in regard to all their sins. He is to do the same for the Tent of Meeting which abides among them, because it is surrounded by their impurities.

No one may be in the Tent of Meeting from the time Aaron goes in to make atonement in the Most Holy Place until he leaves, after he has made atonement for himself, his household, and the whole assembly of Israel.
Then he shall go out to the altar that is before the LORD and make atonement for it. He is to take some of the bull’s blood and some of the goat’s blood and put it on all the horns of the altar.
He is to sprinkle some of the blood on it with his finger seven times to cleanse it and consecrate it from the uncleanness of the Israelites.

media.alt: A goat led out toward the wilderness
media.caption: The live goat carries Israel's confessed sins away into a solitary place.

verses.text: When Aaron has finished purifying the Most Holy Place, the Tent of Meeting, and the altar, he is to bring forward the live goat.

Then he is to lay both hands on the head of the live goat and confess over it all the iniquities and rebellious acts of the Israelites in regard to all their sins. He is to put them on the goat’s head and send it away into the wilderness by the hand of a man appointed for the task.
The goat will carry on itself all their iniquities into a solitary place, and the man will release it into the wilderness.

units.label: Washed, and burned outside the camp

verses.text: Then Aaron is to enter the Tent of Meeting, take off the linen garments he put on before entering the Most Holy Place, and leave them there.

He is to bathe himself with water in a holy place and put on his own clothes. Then he must go out and sacrifice his burnt offering and the people’s burnt offering to make atonement for himself and for the people.
He is also to burn the fat of the sin offering on the altar.
The man who released the goat as the scapegoat must wash his clothes and bathe himself with water; afterward he may reenter the camp.

The bull for the sin offering and the goat for the sin offering, whose blood was brought into the Most Holy Place to make atonement, must be taken outside the camp; and their hides, flesh, and dung must be burned up.
The one who burns them must wash his clothes and bathe himself with water, and afterward he may reenter the camp.
This is to be a permanent statute for you: On the tenth day of the seventh month, you shall humble yourselves and not do any work, whether the native or the foreigner who resides among you,
because on this day atonement will be made for you to cleanse you, and you will be clean from all your sins before the LORD.
It is a Sabbath of complete rest for you, that you may humble yourselves; it is a permanent statute.
The priest who is anointed and ordained to succeed his father as high priest shall make atonement. He will put on the sacred linen garments
and make atonement for the Most Holy Place, the Tent of Meeting, and the altar, and for the priests and all the people of the assembly.
This is to be a permanent statute for you, to make atonement once a year for the Israelites because of all their sins.” And all this was done as the LORD had commanded Moses.

qodesh.gloss: The Most Holy Place, literally holy of holies, the innermost chamber of the tabernacle housing the ark. Only the high priest could enter, only once a year, only with blood, marking it as the point of greatest access to, and greatest danger before, God's presence.

kapporet.gloss: The mercy seat, the golden lid of the ark, from the same root as kaphar, to atone or cover. Blood sprinkled here, before the very place of God's manifest presence, made atonement possible for Israel's worst failures.

kipper.gloss: To atone, to cover, to make amends. Repeated throughout this chapter for the priest, the sanctuary, the altar, and the people, showing that sin defiles more than the sinner, and that a costly, blood based covering is required to deal with it.

azazel.gloss: A term of uncertain origin, traditionally rendered scapegoat, the goat that goes away. Whatever its precise etymology, the ritual meaning is clear: this goat visibly carries Israel's confessed sins away from the camp into a solitary place, never to return.

basic.context: Once a year, on the Day of Atonement, the high priest alone enters the Most Holy Place with the blood of a bull and a goat to atone for himself and the people. A second goat has Israel's sins confessed over it and is sent away into the wilderness, visibly carrying their guilt out of the camp.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real, once a year ritual for Israel's old covenant priesthood, not a pattern Christians repeat. Its significance is what it reveals: sin defiles the sinner, the sanctuary, and the whole community, and only costly, blood based atonement, applied at the point of God's own presence, can deal with it. Hebrews reads the whole ritual as pointing forward to Christ.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter turns on kipper, to atone or cover, applied to the priest, the Most Holy Place, the altar, and the people in turn. The kapporet, mercy seat, gets its name from this same root: it is literally the place of atoning. The second goat, associated with azazel, does not receive blood but confession, and carries sin away bodily.
basic.typology: The two goats together picture one complete work: the first goat's blood satisfies what sin requires at the place of God's presence, and the second goat visibly removes what has been atoned for. Hebrews 9 to 10 reads this whole day as a rehearsal awaiting Christ, who is both the sacrifice whose blood is brought into the true Most Holy Place and the one who bears away sin, accomplished once for all rather than yearly.
basic.christ: Hebrews 9:11-12 says Christ entered the greater tabernacle, not with the blood of goats and calves but with His own blood, having obtained eternal redemption, once for all. He is the reality both goats pictured: His blood atones, and He bears away sin, so that, unlike Aaron, He never needs to repeat the sacrifice.
basic.god: God is so holy that even His own high priest cannot approach carelessly, on pain of death; yet God Himself provides the exact means, blood and confession, by which sinful people are cleansed and He continues to dwell among them. His holiness and His mercy meet in the same ritual.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 9:1-12 draws directly on this chapter to describe Christ's greater and more perfect priestly work. Hebrews 10:1-4 says these sacrifices could never take away sins but only foreshadowed a better one. Psalm 103:12 anticipates the scapegoat's picture: as far as the east is from the west, so far has He removed our transgressions.
basic.oneStory: The Day of Atonement gathers the whole Levitical system into one climactic day: blood applied at the place of God's presence, and sin carried bodily away. Both halves of that picture, atoning blood and the removal of guilt, meet completely in Christ, our great High Priest, who offered Himself once and bore our sins in His own body to the tree.

context.literary:
Leviticus 16 opens by reaching back six chapters. 'After the death of two of Aaron's sons,' verse 1, ties the chapter to Leviticus 10:1-3, where Nadab and Abihu offered unauthorized fire and were consumed. The intervening laws of clean and unclean, chapters 11 to 15, have shown how many ways impurity gathers in a camp where God lives. Chapter 16 is the answer to both problems at once: how a priest may come near without dying, and how a sanctuary soiled by a whole year of impurity can be made fit for God to remain.

The chapter is built in two passes. Verses 3 to 10 give an overview: the animals, the linen clothing, the casting of lots. Verses 11 to 28 then walk through the same rite in detail. The movement of the ritual is from the inside out. Blood is brought first behind the veil, verses 14 and 15, then applied to the Tent of Meeting, verse 16, then to the altar in the court, verses 18 and 19. Only after the whole sanctuary has been purged does the live goat leave the camp, verses 20 to 22. The pattern moves from the throne of God outward to the wilderness, driving uncleanness out along the same path by which it came in.

The warning 'so that he will not die' frames the high priest's entry, verses 2 and 13, and the phrase 'all their sins' recurs like a drumbeat, verses 16, 21, 30 and 34. The closing section, verses 29 to 34, turns from the priest to the people and fixes a date. Many readers note that this chapter stands near the middle of Leviticus, between the laws of sacrifice and purity and the Holiness Code of chapters 17 to 26, as the hinge on which the book turns.
context.historical:
The ritual belongs to Israel's wilderness camp at Sinai, where the tabernacle stood in the middle of the tribes. Its innermost room held the ark, a gold-covered chest containing the stone tablets, verse 13 and Hebrews 9:4, with the golden lid called the mercy seat between the cherubim. There God promised, 'I will meet with you there above the mercy seat,' Exodus 25:22. That promise is exactly what made the room dangerous.

The date is the tenth day of the seventh month, verse 29, in early autumn, five days before the Feast of Tabernacles began on the fifteenth, Leviticus 23:34. It is the only day in the law's calendar on which the whole people are told to humble themselves, and Leviticus 23:29 warns that anyone who will not do so must be cut off. By the first century it was known simply as 'the Fast,' the term Luke uses to date the dangerous season of Paul's voyage, Acts 27:9. The Year of Jubilee was also proclaimed with the ram's horn on this day, Leviticus 25:9, so that release of debts and land began on the day sins were cleansed.

The details would have struck the first hearers. Aaron sets aside the glorious robes made 'to give him glory and splendor,' Exodus 28:2, and wears plain linen. He enters alone, verse 17, while the whole camp waits outside. Two men who handle the goat and the carcasses become unclean by the contact and must bathe before returning, verses 26 and 28. Even the removal of sin leaves its mark on those who carry it out.
context.canonical:
The day is anticipated before it is described. Exodus 30:10 already speaks of atonement made on the horns of the incense altar 'once a year,' and after Leviticus 16 the calendar laws fold it into Israel's festivals, Leviticus 23:26-32 and Numbers 29:7-11. The prophets take up its themes. Isaiah 58:3-5 rebukes a people who 'humbled ourselves' in fasting while oppressing their workers, the very phrase of Leviticus 16:29. Zechariah 3:9 promises that God 'will remove the iniquity of this land in a single day,' language that sounds like a greater Day of Atonement. Micah 7:19 and Psalm 103:12 describe sins cast into the sea and removed as far as east from west, pictures close to the scapegoat's journey.

Isaiah 53 gathers the vocabulary of this chapter onto a person: the LORD 'has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all,' verse 6; He was 'cut off from the land of the living,' verse 8; and 'He bore the sin of many,' verse 12.

The New Testament reads the chapter through Christ. Romans 3:25 calls Him the 'atoning sacrifice,' using the word the Greek Old Testament used for the mercy seat, and Hebrews 9:5 uses the same word for the lid of the ark. Hebrews 9:7 summarises this chapter, the high priest entering 'only once a year, and never without blood,' and Hebrews 9 and 10 build their whole argument on the contrast. Hebrews 13:11-12 draws on verse 27, the bodies burned outside the camp, to interpret Jesus' death 'outside the city gate.' The torn veil at the cross, Matthew 27:51, answers the veil of verse 2.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to grasp that the presence of God in their midst was both their greatest privilege and their gravest danger. The chapter explains why the tabernacle did not simply grow more polluted year by year until God left it. God Himself appointed a day on which every kind of defilement, 'impurities and rebellious acts,' verse 16, was purged from the place of His presence and carried out of the camp.

He also meant the people to take part. The statute of verses 29 to 31 is addressed to 'you,' and it requires them to stop all work and humble themselves. They contribute nothing to the blood rites; they are commanded to rest while the high priest works. The native and the foreigner alike are included, verse 29. The sense is that atonement is received, not achieved, and it is received with humility.

Finally, Moses wanted Israel to trust the result. Verse 30 is one of the most sweeping promises in the law: 'you will be clean from all your sins before the LORD.' The people who had watched the goat go out of sight were meant to live the new year as a cleansed people, confident that God had dealt with what they could not.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is prescriptive for Israel: it is called 'a permanent statute' three times, verses 29, 31 and 34. The Christian question is how a permanent statute is kept when the priesthood and sanctuary it assumes have passed. Hebrews answers that the statute was a shadow, Hebrews 10:1, and that it stands fulfilled rather than abolished: Christ has entered the true Most Holy Place, Hebrews 9:24, and the permanence belongs now to His priesthood, Hebrews 7:24-25. Christians therefore do not repeat the day, and to try would imply His offering was incomplete.

What carries over is the posture the day required. God's people still come to Him humbly, confessing sins specifically, as the high priest confessed them over the goat, verse 21, compare 1 John 1:9. They still rest from their own works to receive a cleansing done by another, Hebrews 4:10. And they are still called to approach God with reverence, though now with confidence, Hebrews 10:19-22.

debates.question: What does the scapegoat, sent to Azazel, represent?

views.label: The goat that goes away
views.case: The Greek Old Testament rendered the term as 'the one sent away,' and William Tyndale's English 'scapegoat,' the goat that escapes, followed this line. On this view Azazel describes the goat's function: it carries the confessed sins away from the camp, matching Psalm 103:12.

views.label: A place in the wilderness
views.case: Some take Azazel as the name of a rugged or remote place, pointing to the 'solitary place' of verse 22. Later Jewish tradition described the goat being led to a cliff in the wilderness. The goat is sent to a land where sin is cut off from Israel for good.

views.label: A wilderness spirit
views.case: Others note the parallel in verse 8, 'one for the LORD and the other for Azazel,' which seems to set a personal name beside God's. Leviticus 17:7 condemns sacrifice to goat demons, and the later book of 1 Enoch names Azazel as a fallen angel. On this view the goat is not an offering to a demon, which the law forbids, but a return of sin to the realm of evil where it belongs.

debates.bearing: Every view agrees on what the ritual does: the goat receives no blood, is not sacrificed, and removes Israel's confessed sin from God's camp beyond return. The New Testament does not settle the term. It simply presents Christ as the one who bears and takes away sin, John 1:29 and Hebrews 9:28.

debates.question: What does kipper, atonement, actually accomplish in this chapter?

views.label: Covering
views.case: The traditional gloss 'cover' fits the mercy seat, the lid over the tablets, and suggests sin hidden from God's sight by blood, an idea Psalm 32:1 expresses with a different verb, 'whose sins are covered.' It captures the idea that guilt is dealt with at the place where God would otherwise meet it in judgment.

views.label: Ransom
views.case: The related noun kopher means a ransom price paid for a life, Exodus 30:12. On this view atonement is substitutionary: a life is given in place of the guilty, which fits Leviticus 17:11 and the death of the animals here.

views.label: Purging or wiping clean
views.case: Many scholars, following Jacob Milgrom's influential work on Leviticus, stress that in chapter 16 kipper is done to objects, the Most Holy Place, the tent and the altar, verse 33. Objects do not sin, so here atonement means purging the sanctuary of the pollution Israel's sins and impurities had deposited in it, verse 19, 'to cleanse it and consecrate it.'

debates.bearing: The chapter holds these together rather than choosing. The sanctuary is purged, verse 16, the people are made clean, verse 30, and it happens only through the death of a substitute whose blood is brought before God. Hebrews likewise speaks of both the purifying of heavenly things, Hebrews 9:23, and the bearing of sins, Hebrews 9:28.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 16 and verse 21 heap up Israel's vocabulary for wrongdoing. Verse 16 speaks of 'impurities,' tum'ot, and 'rebellious acts,' pesha'im, 'in regard to all their sins,' chatto'tam. Verse 21 adds 'iniquities,' avonot. The same three words for iniquity, transgression and sin appear together when God proclaims His name in Exodus 34:7, 'forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin.' Pesha is the strongest of them, the word for revolt against an overlord. Its presence matters, because the ordinary sin offerings of Leviticus 4 dealt with unintentional sins, and Numbers 15:30 says the one who sins defiantly shall be cut off. On this one day even rebellious acts are named and dealt with.

The goat 'will carry on itself all their iniquities,' verse 22, uses nasa avon, to lift or bear iniquity. The phrase can mean to bear guilt as punishment, as in Leviticus 5:1, or to bear it away in forgiveness, and the scapegoat shows the second meaning resting on the first. Isaiah 53:12 uses the same verb of the Servant, 'He bore the sin of many,' and Hebrews 9:28 takes that line up for Christ.

The goat goes to 'a solitary place,' literally 'a land cut off,' from the root gazar, to cut. Isaiah 53:8 uses the same root when it says the Servant 'was cut off from the land of the living.' The echo may be deliberate; at the least the two pictures stand close together.

The people's part is expressed by 'humble yourselves,' verses 29 and 31, which the BSB footnote gives as 'afflict your souls or deny yourselves.' The phrase joins the verb 'anah, to be bowed down or afflicted, with nephesh, the self. Psalm 35:13 pairs it with fasting, 'I humbled myself with fasting,' and Isaiah 58:3-5 shows it had come to mean the fast of this day.

Two superlative constructions frame the chapter. The inner room is qodesh haqodashim, 'holy of holies,' the holiest place, and the day is shabbat shabbaton, 'a Sabbath of complete rest,' verse 31, the most restful of Sabbaths. The holiest place is matched by the holiest rest.

Finally, the Greek Old Testament rendered kapporet, the mercy seat, with hilasterion, the place of atonement. Paul uses that word of Christ in Romans 3:25, 'God presented Him as the atoning sacrifice,' and Hebrews 9:5 uses it of the ark's lid. Behind Paul's statement stands this chapter: God has set forth publicly, at the cross, what was once hidden behind the veil.

typology.type: The high priest entering behind the veil, Leviticus 16:2-17
typology.fulfillment: Aaron went in alone, once a year, first making atonement for his own sins, verse 6, and with blood that was not his own. Hebrews 9:24-25 draws every contrast: Christ entered 'heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God,' not a copy, and not 'every year with blood that is not his own.' He did not need to offer first for Himself, Hebrews 7:27. The escalation is that Aaron came out again and the veil stayed shut, while Christ has gone in as 'our forerunner,' Hebrews 6:20, opening the way for His people to follow, Hebrews 10:19-20. The type falls short most plainly in its repetition, which Hebrews 10:3 calls 'an annual reminder of sins.'

typology.type: The goat for the LORD, whose blood is sprinkled on the mercy seat
typology.fulfillment: The first goat dies and its blood is carried to the place where God appears, cleansing the sanctuary from Israel's sins. Romans 3:25 presents Christ as the hilasterion, the mercy seat itself or the atoning sacrifice offered there, set forth publicly rather than hidden behind a curtain. Hebrews 9:12 says He entered 'by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption,' and Hebrews 9:14 adds that His blood purifies the conscience, which animal blood could not do. The type falls short because the goat was an unwilling animal, while Christ 'offered Himself unblemished to God' through the eternal Spirit.

typology.type: The live goat carrying sins into the wilderness
typology.fulfillment: The confessed sins are placed on the goat's head and carried to a land cut off, never to return. John the Baptist's cry, 'Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world,' John 1:29, uses the language of removal, and Hebrews 9:28 says Christ 'was offered once to bear the sins of many,' echoing Isaiah 53:12. Christ is both goats in one person: He dies, and He bears sin away. The type falls short in that the goat carried Israel's sins for one year only, while Christ 'appeared once for all at the end of the ages to do away with sin,' Hebrews 9:26.

typology.type: The bodies burned outside the camp, Leviticus 16:27
typology.fulfillment: The carcasses of the bull and goat whose blood entered the Most Holy Place were burned outside the camp, a place of uncleanness. Hebrews 13:11-12 makes the connection directly: 'And so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood.' John 19:17 records Him going out, carrying His cross, to Golgotha. The escalation is that the place of rejection becomes the place of holiness, so believers are called to 'go to Him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore,' Hebrews 13:13. The type falls short because the burning was only disposal, while Christ's suffering outside the gate is itself the saving act.

study.christ:
Hebrews 9 and 10 read Leviticus 16 more closely than any other chapter of the Old Testament, and the reading is careful. Hebrews 9:8 says that by this arrangement 'the Holy Spirit was showing that the way into the Most Holy Place had not yet been disclosed as long as the first tabernacle was still standing.' The Day of Atonement did two things at once. It provided real cleansing for Israel, and it announced, by its locked door and its annual repetition, that the final way to God was still to come.

Christ fulfils the priest. Aaron offered first for his own sin, verse 6 and Hebrews 5:3, but Jesus is 'without sin,' Hebrews 4:15, and so needs no bull for Himself, Hebrews 7:27. Aaron laid aside his garments of glory for plain linen to perform this work; the Son laid aside His glory and 'humbled Himself and became obedient to death,' Philippians 2:8. Aaron worked alone while no one else could be in the tent, verse 17; at the cross Jesus was deserted, and the work was His alone.

Christ fulfils the sacrifices. His blood is the blood behind the veil, Hebrews 9:12, and He is the one on whom 'the LORD has laid the iniquity of us all,' Isaiah 53:6, and who carries it away, John 1:29. 2 Corinthians 5:21 says God 'made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf.'

Christ fulfils the place. The mercy seat was where God appeared in the cloud, verse 2; Romans 3:25 says God presented Christ as the atoning sacrifice, the hilasterion, in public view. And when He died, the veil of verse 2 'was torn in two from top to bottom,' Mark 15:38, the direction itself showing that God opened it.

The chapter also shapes how Christians pray. Because the one who entered 'has passed through the heavens,' believers are told to 'approach the throne of grace with confidence,' Hebrews 4:14-16. Aaron entered in dread, shielded by a cloud of incense so that he would not die, verse 13; Christ's people come in by His blood with full assurance, Hebrews 10:22.

A caution belongs here too. Not every item in the ritual is a separate picture of Christ; the number of sprinklings or the type of sash need not be decoded. The links that bear weight are the ones the New Testament itself draws: the priest, the blood, the mercy seat, the veil, the bearing of sin and the place outside the camp.
study.god:
The first thing this chapter reveals about God is that His presence is real and localised, and real presence makes holiness physical. 'I appear in the cloud above the mercy seat,' verse 2. God is not an idea to be approached casually; Nadab and Abihu learned that, Leviticus 10:2-3, and every precaution in this chapter, the bathing, the linen, the incense cloud, exists because God is truly there. Holiness here is not moral strictness in the abstract but the burning purity of the living God among a sinful people.

The chapter shows God's holiness reacting to human sin even at a distance. The Israelites did not enter the sanctuary, yet their impurities and rebellions reached it, so that the tent 'is surrounded by their impurities,' verse 16. Sin is not only a private matter between a person and his conscience; it offends the God who dwells among His people and threatens to drive Him out.

Yet the chapter's deepest word about God is that He wants to stay. The whole ritual exists so that the Tent of Meeting may continue to 'abide among them,' verse 16. God does not solve the problem of sin by leaving. He appoints the means of cleansing, He chooses the goat by lot, verses 8 to 10, and He promises the outcome, 'you will be clean from all your sins before the LORD,' verse 30. Atonement originates with God before it is offered to God.

The chapter holds together justice and mercy without softening either. Sin must be dealt with by death and blood, Hebrews 9:22, and it is not overlooked. But God also provides a second goat so that His people can see their sins go. He is the God of Exodus 34:7, forgiving 'iniquity, transgression, and sin' while not leaving the guilty unpunished, and the Day of Atonement is where those two lines meet in one act.

The chapter also shows God's inclusiveness within His covenant. The foreigner who resides among Israel must humble himself and rest as well, verse 29, and receives the same cleansing. Holiness does not rest on ethnicity but on nearness to the one God.

For worship, the chapter teaches reverence and relief together. God's people should never lose the sense of how costly access to Him is. But they should also know, as Israel knew when the goat was gone, that the God who demands holiness has Himself made them clean.

crossReferences.note: The death of Nadab and Abihu, recalled in Leviticus 16:1, is the reason for the careful procedure of the whole chapter. God's word to Aaron, 'To those who come near Me I will show My holiness,' explains why the high priest may not enter the Most Holy Place freely but only with blood, incense and the prescribed clothing.

God's promise to meet Moses above the mercy seat between the cherubim is the background to Leviticus 16:2, where He appears in the cloud above it. The place of meeting is also the place of danger, which is why the Day of Atonement concentrates its blood rites exactly there.

The festival calendar repeats the Day of Atonement and sharpens its demands on the people: anyone who does not humble himself will be cut off, and the day runs from evening to evening. It shows that the people's part in Leviticus 16:29-31 was not optional but a covenant obligation.

The Servant has the iniquity of all laid on Him, is cut off from the land of the living, and bears the sin of many. The prophet gathers the scapegoat's language of bearing iniquity and the land cut off, Leviticus 16:22, and applies it to a person who suffers and makes intercession.

Paul calls Christ the atoning sacrifice, using the word the Greek Old Testament used for the mercy seat of Leviticus 16. What was hidden behind the veil and approached once a year, God has now presented openly, demonstrating His righteousness at the cross.

The fullest commentary on this chapter. Hebrews notes that only the high priest entered, once a year and never without blood, and that this arrangement signalled the way into the Most Holy Place was not yet open. Christ entered by His own blood and cleanses the conscience, which animal blood could not.

Christ entered heaven itself, not a copy, and did not enter repeatedly with blood not His own as the high priest did every year. He appeared once to do away with sin and was offered once to bear the sins of many, joining the blood of the first goat to the bearing of the second.

The repetition of the Day of Atonement year after year is evidence that it could not perfect the worshipers. The sacrifices served as an annual reminder of sins, since the blood of bulls and goats could not take them away. The chapter's very permanence pointed beyond itself.

Hebrews applies Leviticus 16:27, the bodies burned outside the camp, to Jesus suffering outside the city gate. It then calls believers to go to Him outside the camp, turning the place of disposal and uncleanness into the place of fellowship with Christ in His disgrace.

At the moment Jesus breathed His last, the veil of the temple was torn from top to bottom. The curtain that Leviticus 16:2 forbade Aaron to pass freely is opened by God Himself, and the once a year entry gives way to access through Christ.

God promises to remove the iniquity of the land in a single day. Set against the annual Day of Atonement, the promise looks for a day of cleansing that will not need repeating, which Hebrews 10:12-14 finds in the single offering of Christ.

David measures forgiveness by the horizon, the widest distance an Israelite could imagine. The psalm turns into praise what the scapegoat acted out every autumn: confessed sins taken to a place from which they never find their way back, and the link is made by the same idea of distance, not by shared vocabulary.

study.oneStory:
The first sanctuary in Scripture was a garden, and it ended with a guarded entrance: cherubim stationed on the east side of Eden to keep the way to the tree of life, Genesis 3:24. The tabernacle repeats that picture. Cherubim are worked over the mercy seat, and the way into the innermost room is barred to all but one man on one day. Leviticus 16 answers the question the fall left hanging: can sinners ever come back into God's presence? The answer is yes, but only through a priest, a death, and blood brought before God.

The chapter also answers the problem the book of Exodus raised. God came down to dwell among Israel, Exodus 40:34, and Leviticus 26:11-12 will promise, 'I will walk among you and be your God.' But a holy God living among an unclean people would either consume them or be driven away. The Day of Atonement is the provision that makes the promise of presence sustainable year after year.

It sets up much of what follows. Israel's history shows that the ritual could cleanse the sanctuary but not change the heart; Isaiah 58 finds the people keeping the fast while oppressing the poor, and the prophets look for a day when God will remove iniquity once and cleanse His people from within, Zechariah 3:9 and Ezekiel 36:25. Isaiah 53 promises a Servant who will bear iniquity Himself.

The story reaches its turning point in Christ, who fulfils the priest, the sacrifice and the scapegoat in one life and one death. The torn veil means the approach to God that Leviticus 16 rationed is now open to all who come by His blood, Hebrews 10:19-20.

The new creation completes the pattern. John sees the ark of the covenant in God's heavenly temple, Revelation 11:19, and then a city with no temple at all, 'because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22. There will be no annual day of cleansing there, because there will be nothing unclean left to remove, and no veil, because God's people 'will see His face,' Revelation 22:4.

quiz.q: Why does the chapter open by recalling the death of Aaron's two sons?

options.text: To warn that Aaron himself must not enter the Most Holy Place freely, or he too will die.
options.note: Verses 1-2 draw this connection explicitly.

options.text: To explain who would replace them as priests.
options.note: The text's stated concern is the manner of entering God's presence, not succession.

options.text: It is unrelated background information.
options.note: Verse 2 directly ties the warning to what happened to Nadab and Abihu.

options.text: To celebrate their memory.
options.note: The passage uses their death as a solemn warning, not a celebration.

quiz.q: What happened to the two goats chosen by lot?

options.text: One was sacrificed as a sin offering; the other was sent alive into the wilderness bearing the people's sins.
options.note: Verses 8-10 and 15, 20-22 describe this two part ritual.

options.text: Both were sacrificed on the altar together.
options.note: Only one goat was slaughtered; the other was released alive.

options.text: Both were released into the wilderness.
options.note: Only the scapegoat was released; the other goat was sacrificed as a sin offering.

options.text: The text does not distinguish between the two goats.
options.note: Verses 8-10 explicitly assign each goat a distinct role by lot.

quiz.q: What did Aaron do with the blood of the bull and the goat behind the veil?

options.text: He sprinkled it on and before the mercy seat to make atonement for himself, his household, and the people.
options.note: Verses 14-16 describe this sprinkling in detail.

options.text: He poured it out entirely at the base of the altar outside the tent.
options.note: The blood was sprinkled specifically before the mercy seat inside the veil, not merely poured outside.

options.text: He drank a portion of it as part of the ritual.
options.note: Leviticus elsewhere forbids consuming blood; it is applied to the mercy seat and altar, never consumed.

options.text: No blood was brought behind the veil.
options.note: Verses 14-15 explicitly describe blood brought and sprinkled behind the veil.

quiz.q: What did Aaron do over the head of the live goat before it was released?

options.text: He laid both hands on it and confessed all the iniquities of the Israelites over it.
options.note: Verse 21 describes this confession and laying on of hands.

options.text: He slaughtered it as a burnt offering.
options.note: The live goat was not slaughtered; it was released alive into the wilderness.

options.text: He simply released it without any ceremony.
options.note: Verse 21 specifically describes the laying on of hands and confession before release.

options.text: Nothing is recorded about this goat.
options.note: Verses 20-22 describe this goat's role in detail.

quiz.q: According to Hebrews, how does Christ's priestly work compare to what happens in this chapter?

options.text: Christ entered the true, heavenly sanctuary once for all with His own blood, obtaining eternal redemption, unlike the yearly entry of Israel's high priest.
options.note: Hebrews 9:11-12, 24-26 makes this contrast directly.

options.text: Christ repeats His sacrifice every year just as Aaron did.
options.note: Hebrews 10:10 stresses the opposite: Christ's offering was made once for all, not repeated.

options.text: Hebrews never connects Christ's work to this chapter.
options.note: Hebrews 9 draws extensively and directly on the Day of Atonement to describe Christ's priesthood.

options.text: Hebrews treats this chapter as having no ongoing significance.
options.note: Hebrews treats this chapter as central to understanding Christ's atoning work.

questions: Aaron could not enter God's presence carelessly, only by the exact way God prescribed. Where are you tempted to approach God casually, on your own terms, rather than through the way He has provided in Christ?

The first goat's blood satisfied what sin required; the second goat visibly carried sin away. Which of these truths, that your sin is atoned for, or that it is genuinely removed, do you find harder to believe about yourself right now?
Aaron had to make atonement for himself before he could make it for the people. Where do you need to acknowledge your own need before you are quick to address the sins of others?

This whole elaborate, costly ritual had to be repeated every single year, and still could not perfect anyone's conscience. How does knowing that Christ's one sacrifice is enough change the way you carry guilt this week?

The scapegoat carried Israel's confessed sins into a solitary place, never to return. Is there a sin or a failure you keep dragging back into the camp of your own mind, even though Christ has already carried it away?

translationNotes.note: Mercy seat translates kapporet, the golden lid of the ark, sharing its root with kaphar, to atone; some render it simply as the atonement cover, making the wordplay with the whole chapter's theme explicit.

Scapegoat translates the Hebrew azazel, a term of debated origin; whether it names a place, a being, or simply describes the goat's function, the ritual sense is unaffected: this goat visibly bears sin away from the camp.

Humble yourselves is the law's language for what later Judaism calls fasting on Yom Kippur; the text itself does not use the specific word for fasting, but the demand for self affliction was understood that way from an early date.
